title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 53
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: A Machine for Making Notes
passages.text:
A. The piano was invented to solve a problem of loudness control rather than of pitch. Keyboard instruments before it either plucked the string, giving the same volume however the key was struck, or were too quiet to lead an ensemble; an instrument in which a hammer strikes the string and immediately falls away lets the player vary loudness with the finger, and that single capability is what the name records.

B. The mechanism required to do this is more intricate than the sound suggests. A hammer must be thrown at the string rather than pushed, so that it is travelling freely when it arrives and can rebound instead of damping what it has just struck; it must then be caught, held ready, and returned so the note can be repeated quickly. The linkage that achieves this contains dozens of parts per key and was refined over a century of small changes.

C. Tension is the reason the instrument looks as it does. Strings pulled tight enough for the volume expected of a concert instrument exert a combined force of many tonnes, and a wooden frame cannot resist it for long without distorting. The iron frame that solved this made the modern instrument possible and made it extremely heavy, which determined where pianos could be put and how their music would be performed.

D. The most consequential decision was made before any of this and is rarely noticed. Dividing the octave into twelve equal steps allows an instrument to play in every key at the cost of no key being exactly in tune, and a fixed-pitch instrument must make some such compromise because it cannot adjust as it plays. What sounds to modern listeners like simply being in tune is a specific historical settlement.

E. The industry that produced these instruments was one of the largest manufacturing sectors of its time and has almost vanished. Domestic demand was enormous while a piano was the only way to have music at home, and it collapsed when recording and broadcasting made that unnecessary; the firms that survived did so by concentrating on the small professional market, and the skills involved became scarce enough to be a constraint.

F. What has kept the instrument in use is a property nobody designed. Its interface is visible, its layout makes the structure of the music explicit to the eye, and a beginner can produce a correct note immediately in a way that string and wind instruments do not allow. It survived the disappearance of its market because it turned out to be the best available machine for thinking about music.

passages.title: Holes in the Rock
passages.text:
Caves in limestone are made by water that is very slightly acidic, working over periods that make the process invisible. Rainwater takes up carbon dioxide from the air and from soil, becomes a weak acid, and dissolves calcium carbonate as it passes through joints in the rock; the joint widens, more water follows the easier route, and the widening accelerates. What begins as a network of cracks becomes a drainage system, and eventually a passage a person can walk along.

The landscape above records the same process. Where limestone lies at the surface, water disappears into it rather than running across it, so rivers vanish into holes, valleys are dry, hollows form where cavities beneath have collapsed, and springs emerge at the base of the formation carrying water that entered kilometres away. The surface and the underground are a single system, which has consequences that are more practical than scenic.

The practical consequence is that such landscapes have almost no natural filtration. Water entering a swallow hole reaches a spring in hours or days rather than the months or years it would take to percolate through sand or clay, and it arrives having been filtered by very little. Contamination that would be diluted and degraded elsewhere emerges essentially intact, and settlements drawing water from such springs are exposed in a way that is easy to underestimate.

The formations inside are deposits rather than erosion and grow slowly. Water carrying dissolved carbonate loses carbon dioxide when it reaches an air-filled space, and can no longer hold what it is carrying, so a small amount of mineral is left behind at each drip point. Growth rates are typically a fraction of a millimetre a year, which is why damage to these structures is permanent on any human timescale and why the layers they contain are a usable record of past climate.

Cave life is shaped by the absence of light and of any local production. Nothing photosynthesises in a cave, so the energy comes from outside — washed in as organic material, carried in by animals that leave to feed, or in some systems produced by bacteria using chemical energy — and the resulting communities are sparse, slow and highly specialised. Species confined to a single cave system are common, which makes them unusually easy to eliminate.

Exploration remains one of the few fields where the map is genuinely blank. Passages are found by people crawling into them, remote sensing works poorly through rock, and there is no way to know what a system contains without entering it. The result is a science in which amateur explorers still make the primary discoveries, and in which the survey drawn by whoever went first is often the only record that exists.

passages.title: Insuring the Weather
passages.text:
A farmer whose crop fails from drought faces the same loss as one whose warehouse burns, and until recently could not insure against it in most of the world. The obstacle is that conventional insurance requires someone to visit and assess each claim, which is affordable for a building and not for a hectare of maize a long way from a road, and the sums involved are too small to carry that cost.

Index insurance was designed around that problem by changing what triggers payment. Instead of assessing the actual loss, the contract pays when a measurable index crosses a threshold — rainfall at a nearby station below a specified amount, or a satellite measure of vegetation below a specified value — and payment follows automatically without anyone inspecting anything. The administrative cost collapses, and with it the reason such insurance could not exist.

The design introduces a specific failure that has no equivalent in ordinary insurance. The index may not match the individual farm: rain may fall at the measuring station and not on the field, so the farmer loses the crop and receives nothing, and the reverse can also occur. This gap between the index and the actual loss is the product's central weakness, it cannot be eliminated, and it is the main reason farmers who try the product often do not renew.

Take-up has been persistently lower than the theoretical case predicts, and the reasons are now reasonably well understood. Farmers must pay before a season they may not survive financially; the product is difficult to explain and requires trusting a payout rule rather than a person; a single experience of losing a crop and receiving nothing destroys confidence more thoroughly than several correct payments build it; and existing informal arrangements between neighbours already cover part of the risk.

What the insurance changes, when it works, is behaviour rather than income. A household that knows a catastrophic year will be partly covered will plant a higher-yielding but more drought-sensitive variety, apply fertiliser, and invest in ways it would not otherwise risk — and the measured gains come mostly from those decisions rather than from the payouts themselves. The value is in removing the need to farm defensively.

The realistic assessment is that this is a useful instrument and not a solution to agricultural poverty. It works best bundled with credit or inputs rather than sold alone, it requires subsidy at the premiums smallholders can pay, and it addresses one risk among several that such households face. Presenting it as a market solution requiring no public money has been the main obstacle to its being deployed in the form that actually works.
